question.en:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in the correct order.

The old lighthouse keeper

P. that guided fishing boats

Q. climbed the spiral stairs each evening

R. safely into the harbour

S. to light the lamp

solution_text.en:
Opener test.

The old lighthouse keeper is the subject; it needs a verb next. Only Q (climbed…) has a main verb. So Q comes first.

Links.

• Q → S: climbed the stairs to light the lamp: the to-infinitive gives the purpose.

• S → P: that needs a noun to refer to; the lamp that guided fishing boats.

• P → R: guided fishing boats safely into the harbour: 'guide… into' completes the phrase.

Order: Q S P R

The sentence.

The old lighthouse keeper climbed the spiral stairs each evening to light the lamp that guided fishing boats safely into the harbour.

Subject → verb → purpose → relative clause → where: the usual English sentence flow.

question.en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The new policy does not address rural unemployment, and it does not offer any relief to small traders ________.

solution_text.en:
Rule: Also / too add a point in affirmative sentences. When the added point is negative, use either at the end of the clause.

Example: Ravi likes tea; his sister likes it too. → Ravi doesn't like tea; his sister doesn't like it either.

(नकारात्मक वाक्य में 'भी' के लिए either)

Apply it.

Both clauses are negative: does not address… does not offer…

The second negative adds to the first, so it ends with either.

→ …and it does not offer any relief to small traders either.

Why the others are wrong.

• also: used with affirmative ideas; 'does not offer… also' is wrong.

• too: same problem; 'too' in this sense belongs to affirmative sentences.

• neither: already negative. Placed after 'does not', it creates a double negative (not… neither).

Answer: either

Spot the 'not' in the second clause first: positive → also/too; negative → either.

question.en:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (1).

Meena is the first person in her family to set foot in a college. Her father drives an auto-rickshaw and her mother stitches school uniforms, and neither of them studied beyond Class 8. When her admission letter arrived, the whole street came to congratulate her, but the joy was soon _____(1) by worry. Who would explain the fee forms, the scholarship portals and the long lectures in English?

In her first semester, Meena often felt like an outsider. Classmates chatted easily about internships and coaching classes, while she quietly _____(2) the meaning of terms they took for granted. She did not lack ability; she lacked a map. Teachers who have worked with students like her say that it is high time colleges _____(3) such learners as an asset rather than a burden, and offered them mentoring from the very first day.

Meena found her own mentor in a senior who had once stood where she stood. He showed her how to _____(4) the library, the help desk and the free evening classes. By her final year, she was guiding new students herself. Her parents still cannot read her textbooks, but they know that she has (5) broken new ground for the family.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (1).

solution_text.en:
"…the whole street came to congratulate her, but the joy was soon tempered by worry."

tempered (by) = made less strong; balanced or softened by something else (कम/मंद हो जाना)

Her joy did not vanish, but worry about fees and lectures reduced it. Joy tempered by worry is a natural collocation.

Why the others are wrong.

• tampered = interfered with something to damage it (छेड़छाड़ करना); it takes 'with' and does not fit 'joy… by worry'. It only looks like 'tempered'.

• hastened = made to happen sooner (जल्दी कराना): worry does not speed up joy.

• prompted = caused or encouraged (प्रेरित करना): worry did not cause the joy.

Answer: tempered

'But' signals a contrast: joy reduced by worry → tempered.

question.en:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (2).

Meena is the first person in her family to set foot in a college. Her father drives an auto-rickshaw and her mother stitches school uniforms, and neither of them studied beyond Class 8. When her admission letter arrived, the whole street came to congratulate her, but the joy was soon _____(1) by worry. Who would explain the fee forms, the scholarship portals and the long lectures in English?

In her first semester, Meena often felt like an outsider. Classmates chatted easily about internships and coaching classes, while she quietly _____(2) the meaning of terms they took for granted. She did not lack ability; she lacked a map. Teachers who have worked with students like her say that it is high time colleges _____(3) such learners as an asset rather than a burden, and offered them mentoring from the very first day.

Meena found her own mentor in a senior who had once stood where she stood. He showed her how to _____(4) the library, the help desk and the free evening classes. By her final year, she was guiding new students herself. Her parents still cannot read her textbooks, but they know that she has (5) broken new ground for the family.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (2).

solution_text.en:
"…while she quietly looked up the meaning of terms they took for granted."

look up (a word / meaning) = to search for information in a dictionary, book or phone (शब्द का अर्थ खोजना)

Meena did not know the terms her classmates used, so she searched for their meaning on her own.

Why the others are wrong.

• looked after = took care of (देखभाल करना).

• looked down on = regarded as inferior (तुच्छ समझना).

• looked forward to = waited eagerly for (उत्सुकता से प्रतीक्षा करना).

Answer: looked up

Word help. take for granted (मान कर चलना, सामान्य समझना)

Phrasal verbs with 'look': up = search, after = care, down on = despise, forward to = eagerly wait.

question.en:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (3).

Meena is the first person in her family to set foot in a college. Her father drives an auto-rickshaw and her mother stitches school uniforms, and neither of them studied beyond Class 8. When her admission letter arrived, the whole street came to congratulate her, but the joy was soon _____(1) by worry. Who would explain the fee forms, the scholarship portals and the long lectures in English?

In her first semester, Meena often felt like an outsider. Classmates chatted easily about internships and coaching classes, while she quietly _____(2) the meaning of terms they took for granted. She did not lack ability; she lacked a map. Teachers who have worked with students like her say that it is high time colleges _____(3) such learners as an asset rather than a burden, and offered them mentoring from the very first day.

Meena found her own mentor in a senior who had once stood where she stood. He showed her how to _____(4) the library, the help desk and the free evening classes. By her final year, she was guiding new students herself. Her parents still cannot read her textbooks, but they know that she has (5) broken new ground for the family.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (3).

solution_text.en:
Rule: It is time / It is high time / It is about time + subject is followed by the simple past (subjunctive) form, even though the meaning is present or future. The other pattern is It is high time for + object + to-infinitive.

Example: It is high time we started work. / It is high time for us to start work.

(It is high time के बाद भूतकाल का रूप)

Apply it.

…it is high time colleges recognised such learners as an asset… and offered them mentoring…

The second verb in the same clause, offered, is already in the past form, which confirms the pattern.

Why the others are wrong.

• recognise: present form; after 'it is high time + subject' the verb must be past.

• had recognised: past perfect is not used in this structure.

• will recognise: future form is never used after 'it is high time'.

Answer: recognised

'High time' means it should already have happened, so the verb goes into the past.

question.en:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (4).

Meena is the first person in her family to set foot in a college. Her father drives an auto-rickshaw and her mother stitches school uniforms, and neither of them studied beyond Class 8. When her admission letter arrived, the whole street came to congratulate her, but the joy was soon _____(1) by worry. Who would explain the fee forms, the scholarship portals and the long lectures in English?

In her first semester, Meena often felt like an outsider. Classmates chatted easily about internships and coaching classes, while she quietly _____(2) the meaning of terms they took for granted. She did not lack ability; she lacked a map. Teachers who have worked with students like her say that it is high time colleges _____(3) such learners as an asset rather than a burden, and offered them mentoring from the very first day.

Meena found her own mentor in a senior who had once stood where she stood. He showed her how to _____(4) the library, the help desk and the free evening classes. By her final year, she was guiding new students herself. Her parents still cannot read her textbooks, but they know that she has (5) broken new ground for the family.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (4).

solution_text.en:
"He showed her how to make use of the library, the help desk and the free evening classes."

make use of = to use something available to one's advantage (का उपयोग करना, लाभ उठाना)

The senior showed her how to benefit from the facilities the college already had.

Why the others are wrong.

• make up for = to compensate for a loss or mistake (की भरपाई करना).

• make away with = to steal and run off with (चुराकर भाग जाना).

• make out of = to produce something from a material (से बनाना), as in a bag made out of jute.

Answer: make use of

Library, help desk, evening classes: all are facilities you 'make use of'.

option_1.en: She has damaged the family's good name by leaving home for college.

option_2.en: She has bought a plot of land for the family with her first salary.

option_3.en: She has started farming a field that her family had never tilled.

option_4.en: She has achieved something no one in her family had done before.

question.en:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Meena is the first person in her family to set foot in a college. Her father drives an auto-rickshaw and her mother stitches school uniforms, and neither of them studied beyond Class 8. When her admission letter arrived, the whole street came to congratulate her, but the joy was soon _____(1) by worry. Who would explain the fee forms, the scholarship portals and the long lectures in English?

In her first semester, Meena often felt like an outsider. Classmates chatted easily about internships and coaching classes, while she quietly _____(2) the meaning of terms they took for granted. She did not lack ability; she lacked a map. Teachers who have worked with students like her say that it is high time colleges _____(3) such learners as an asset rather than a burden, and offered them mentoring from the very first day.

Meena found her own mentor in a senior who had once stood where she stood. He showed her how to _____(4) the library, the help desk and the free evening classes. By her final year, she was guiding new students herself. Her parents still cannot read her textbooks, but they know that she has (5) broken new ground for the family.

In the context of the passage, what does the phrase 'broken new ground' (5) suggest about Meena?

solution_text.en:
"Her parents still cannot read her textbooks, but they know that she has broken new ground for the family."

break new ground = to do something that has not been done before (नई राह खोलना, पहली बार कुछ करना)

The passage opens with "Meena is the first person in her family to set foot in a college". She is the first to reach college and now guides others, so she has done what no one in her family did before.

Why the others are wrong.

• Damaged the family's good name: 'broken' here is not harm; the passage is full of pride, and the family is proud of her college life.

• Bought a plot of land: takes 'ground' literally; no land or salary is mentioned.

• Started farming a field never tilled before: again reads 'break ground' as digging soil (ज़मीन जोतना), the literal sense.

Answer: She has achieved something no one in her family had done before.

Origin. Farmers 'broke ground' when they ploughed land never tilled before; the phrase came to mean doing something new for the first time.

When an idiom appears in a passage, test it against the opening line; here 'first person in her family' settles it.

option_1.en: The coach said to Ritu, "Why did you look so tired this morning?"

option_2.en: The coach said to Ritu, "Why do you look so tired this morning?"

option_3.en: The coach said to Ritu, "Why do you look so tired that morning?"

option_4.en: The coach said to Ritu, "Why you look so tired this morning?"

question.en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech.

The coach asked Ritu why she looked so tired that morning.

solution_text.en:
Rule: In indirect speech a wh-question is reported as asked + wh-word + subject + verb (statement order, no 'that', no question mark). To go back to direct speech, reverse every change: restore question order (wh-word + auxiliary + subject + verb), move the tense one step forward and turn 'that' time words back into 'this'.

Example: She asked me where I lived. → She said to me, "Where do you live?"

(प्रश्नवाचक वाक्य का प्रत्यक्ष कथन)

Apply it.

The coach asked Ritu why she looked so tired that morning.

• asked → said to

• she → you (Ritu is the listener)

• looked → do you look (question order + simple present)

• that morning → this morning

Why the others are wrong.

• "Why did you look…" keeps the past tense. Simple past in reported speech goes back to simple present in direct speech.

• "…that morning?" keeps the reported time word; it must return to 'this'.

• "Why you look…" has statement order. A direct wh-question needs the auxiliary 'do' before the subject.

Answer: The coach said to Ritu, "Why do you look so tired this morning?"

Indirect → direct: question order back, tense one step forward, 'that' → 'this'.

option_3.en: In apposition to a noun

question.en:
Select the option that correctly identifies the function of the underlined clause in the given sentence.

The rumour that the examination had been postponed caused panic among the candidates.

solution_text.en:
Rule: A noun clause (संज्ञा उपवाक्य) does the work of a noun. Find its job by asking what it stands for in the sentence:

• it does the action → subject of the verb (क्रिया का कर्ता)

• it receives the action → object of the verb (क्रिया का कर्म)

• it follows of, about, on → object of a preposition (पूर्वसर्ग का कर्म)

• it comes right after a noun such as fact, news, belief, rumour and tells us what that noun is → in apposition to the noun (संज्ञा का समानाधिकरण)

Test for apposition: the clause is complete in itself, and you can write noun = clause.

Example: The fact that she resigned surprised us. → the fact = she resigned.

Do not confuse it with a relative (adjective) clause (विशेषण उपवाक्य): in The rumour that he spread was false, 'that' = which, and 'spread' has lost its object. That clause describes the rumour; it does not state it.

Apply it.

The rumour that the examination had been postponed caused panic among the candidates.

• The clause is complete: the examination had been postponed (subject + verb, nothing missing).

• It tells us what the rumour was: the rumour = the examination had been postponed.

So it is a noun clause in apposition to the noun rumour.

Why the others are wrong.

• Subject of the verb: the subject of caused is the rumour; the clause only explains that noun. Remove the clause and The rumour caused panic still has its subject.

• Object of the verb: the object of caused is panic, not the clause.

• Object of a preposition: no preposition comes before the clause; among governs the candidates.

Answer: In apposition to a noun

Word help. postponed (स्थगित), panic (घबराहट)

Noun + 'that' + a complete sentence = apposition; noun + 'that' + a sentence with a gap = relative clause.

option_1.en: The officer gave us an information that completely changed our travel plans.

option_2.en: My uncle offered me a valuable piece of advice before the interview.

option_3.en: The college has bought a new furniture for the conference hall.

option_4.en: She dragged a heavy luggage all the way up the stairs.

question.en: Select the grammatically correct sentence.

solution_text.en:
Rule: Uncountable nouns such as advice, information, news, furniture, luggage, knowledge, equipment have no plural and never take a/an. To count them, use a unit word: a piece of advice, an item of news, a piece of furniture, a bag of luggage.

Example: She gave me some advice. / She gave me a piece of advice. (not an advice)

(अगणनीय संज्ञा के साथ a/an नहीं लगता)

Apply it.

My uncle offered me a valuable piece of advice before the interview.

Here 'a' goes with piece (countable), not with 'advice'. The sentence is correct.

Why the others are wrong.

• an information → some information / a piece of information

• a new furniture → new furniture / a new piece of furniture

• a heavy luggage → heavy luggage / a heavy bag

Answer: My uncle offered me a valuable piece of advice before the interview.

Adding an adjective (valuable, new, heavy) does not make an uncountable noun countable.
